thesis_points: First publicly traded land banking REIT — 876 communities, 139,000 homesites, $8.4B homesite inventory under option

IROIC (9.5–10.3%) exceeds WACC; value-accretive at current P/BV of ~0.87x; book value grows as inventory expands
HOPP'R technology platform (centralized land analytics + deal execution) creates a moat difficult to replicate at scale
Consensus analyst: 'Land is land — unless there's a recession, no reason to trade at a discount to book'

key_debate.street: Lennar concentration risk (80% revenue); limited operating history makes walkaway risk difficult to price; housing macro headwinds

overview.narrative:
REITs sold off broadly on July 8, with only Tower holding flat at -0.00% while Hospitality (-2.27%), Housing (-2.36%), and Office (-1.99%) bore the brunt of the selling. The risk-off tone appears driven by renewed rate anxiety, hitting duration-sensitive and economically-cyclical names hardest. SPG cratered -3.57%, HPP fell -4.43%, and NXRT dropped -4.70%, reflecting particular pressure on names with near-term refinancing exposure and weaker tenant fundamentals.

The divergence between Tower resilience and the rest of the complex is notable — UNIT's +1.21% gain and SBAC's modest -0.68% decline suggest investors are hiding in contracted-cashflow, inflation-linked models. IIPR's +1.71% outperformance stands out as an idiosyncratic story amid broad Industrial weakness (-1.22%), with COLD's -3.26% decline suggesting cold storage sentiment has turned. Healthcare lagged expectations with ARE dropping -2.77%, likely reflecting ongoing life science space concerns. The -2.63% print in GLPI within Netlease warrants attention given gaming REIT fundamentals remain solid, suggesting forced selling or technical pressure.

Positioning into Wednesday should favor defensive, contracted-revenue names — Towers and select Netlease. We would fade any bounce in Office and Hospitality absent a clear catalyst. Watch the 10-year closely; another leg higher in yields could accelerate rotation out of Housing and Retail into shorter-duration plays.
